clue.text: Ruin county initially for everybody

indicators.note: what comes initially is at the start, so only the opening letter of the next word is used

blocks.note: Down is a county of Northern Ireland
the opening letter of this word
everybody is all of them

explanation.surface: Someone complains that a county's early decision will ruin life for all its residents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initially' seems to describe when the ruin happened, but it only picks the first letter of 'for'. County Down is one of the six counties of Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: A downfall is a collapse or loss of fortune, which is exactly what ruin means as a noun.

clue.text: It’s pretty, and it changed by the end of July

indicators.note: something changed has been altered, so the letters are rearranged
the end of a word is its final letter, so only that letter is kept

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
the closing letter of the month

explanation.surface: A dress looks pretty, and it was altered in time for a summer wedding at the end of July.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And it' reads as ordinary grammar but is the fodder; 'by' just attaches the final Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Dainty describes something delicately small and graceful, a close synonym for pretty as an adjective.

clue.text: Naughty wife chose to go topless

indicators.note: going topless means losing the top, and in a down entry the top is the first letter, so it is removed

blocks.note: W is the standard abbreviation for wife
to choose is to pick

explanation.surface: A naughty wife decides to go topless on the beach.
explanation.walkthrough: The racy picture hides a simple removal: the word for 'chose' loses its first letter, P, before W is placed in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Wicked and naughty both describe bad or mischievous behaviour, making them straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: This writer's neglected himself, running up fat

indicators.note: what is neglected is left out, so those letters are dropped
in a down entry, running up means reading from bottom to top, so the letters turn around

blocks.note: the setter refers to themselves; 'this writer is' becomes I'M
taken as written

explanation.surface: A writer admits to neglecting his health and piling on the pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This writer's' is the setter speaking: I'M. Take I'M out of HIMSELF to leave HSELF, then read it upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Flesh is the soft tissue of the body, and in particular its fat, as in someone putting on flesh.

clue.text: The Parisian children's schoolwork

blocks.note: les is French for 'the' (plural), as used in Paris
sons are children

explanation.surface: Parents discuss the homework their French children bring home.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s looks possessive but is 'is', joining wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Lessons are the periods of teaching and tasks that make up school study, a fair match for schoolwork.

clue.text: Corpulent woman's old man

blocks.note: corpulent means fat
a woman's thing is hers; HER stands for the woman

explanation.surface: A description of a stout woman's husband or partner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old man' sounds like the woman's husband, which it can be in slang, but here it is the familiar term for a dad.
explanation.definitionFit: 'My old man' is an informal British way of referring to one's dad or male parent.

clue.text: Class with mites in it had arnica cultivated

indicators.note: cultivated ground is worked over and turned, so the letters are dug over into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A garden bed of arnica plants was grown, but the class of pupils found mites in it.
explanation.walkthrough: Arnica is a medicinal plant, so 'cultivated' reads naturally as gardening before it becomes the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Arachnida is the zoological class containing spiders, scorpions, ticks and mites.

clue.text: Labour strongman, he's stashed money raised

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising something lifts it to read bottom to top, so it runs backwards
to stash is to hide something away inside, so one piece is tucked within the other

blocks.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe
lucre is money, especially ill-gotten

explanation.surface: A Labour party heavyweight is caught hiding money he has raised in funds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' looks political, but it refers to the twelve labours of the Greek hero. The reversed money word goes between the H and the ES.
explanation.definitionFit: Hercules, famous for his great strength, performed twelve labours as penance in Greek mythology.

clue.text: Don’t forget scripture branch

blocks.note: RE is religious education, the school subject once called scripture
a member is a limb or branch

explanation.surface: A reminder not to leave out a branch of scripture study.
explanation.walkthrough: RE (religious education) is the British school subject, formerly called scripture or RI.
explanation.definitionFit: To remember is to keep in mind, the positive form of the instruction not to forget.

clue.text: Augment batting?

blocks.note: first meaning: to make larger
second meaning, split into two words: a batsman in cricket stands in the crease

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the word as IN CREASE: in cricket the crease is the line where the batsman stands, so a batting player is in (the) crease.
explanation.definitionFit: To increase something is to make it bigger, a direct synonym for augment as a verb.

clue.text: One in meeting at Murrayfield needs backbone

definitions.note: the sacrum is part of the backbone rather than the whole of it

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: one is 'a', the indefinite article
Murrayfield is the Scottish rugby stadium in Edinburgh, where the forwards meet in a scrum

explanation.surface: A rugby player locked in the scrum at Murrayfield needs a strong back.
explanation.walkthrough: Murrayfield is the home of Scottish rugby in Edinburgh, so the 'meeting' there is a scrum, where the packs bind together.
explanation.definitionFit: The sacrum is the triangular bone at the base of the spine, a fused section of the vertebral column.

clue.text: Disarm group of upstanding gentlemen

indicators.note: a group of letters is a run lifted from inside the following word
in a down entry, standing up means reading from the bottom upwards, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: four consecutive letters from the middle of this word

explanation.surface: A call to disarm a band of respectable, upright gentlemen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upstanding' reads as a compliment to the gentlemen but tells you to read the run of letters upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To melt someone is to soften their heart or resistance, just as to disarm is to win over by charm.

clue.text: Put monarch ultimately thereon, unsteadily

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so only the final letters of the preceding words are used
something placed unsteadily wobbles out of place, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the closing letters of these two words
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An awkward coronation: the king is finally installed, a little shakily, on the seat of power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultimately' applies to both 'Put' and 'monarch', giving T and H; these join the letters of 'thereon' for the rearrangement. Read whole, the clue says where a monarch is eventually put.
explanation.definitionFit: The throne is the royal seat on which a sovereign is placed at a coronation, so it is where one puts a monarch.

clue.text: Spoils first of Maggie Thatcher's material

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, so only that letter is taken

blocks.note: a haul is the spoils or loot taken
the opening letter of the name

explanation.surface: Something spoils the early political writings of Margaret Thatcher, the former prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maggie Thatcher' looks like one name, but the surname becomes a roof thatcher, whose raw material is straw.
explanation.definitionFit: Haulm is the stalks or stems of crops such as beans and peas, used as straw for roofing and bedding.

clue.text: Does exploit dwellings abandoned by Home Office

indicators.note: what is abandoned is left behind, so those letters leave the word

blocks.note: houses are dwellings
HO is the abbreviation for the Home Office, the UK government department for policing and immigration

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the government exploits homes left empty by the Home Office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Does' looks like the start of a question but is part of the definition. The Home Office is the British ministry for policing and immigration.
explanation.definitionFit: Uses and does exploit are both third-person present verbs meaning makes use of or takes advantage of.

clue.text: Pieces of ceramic protect hard disk guides

indicators.note: to protect something is to surround and shield it, so one piece wraps around the other

blocks.note: sherds (or shards) are broken fragments of pottery
an EP, an extended-play record, is a disc
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: Fragments of ceramic are used to protect a computer's hard disk, as the installation guides explain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard disk' reads as one computer part, but it splits into two pieces, and they go in with the disk first. Sherd is the archaeologist's spelling of shard.
explanation.definitionFit: To shepherd people is to steer and lead them along, so shepherds works as a verb meaning guides.

clue.text: Announced attempt with soldiers in old boat

indicators.note: something announced is spoken out loud, so a word is given by its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: an attempt is a try
REME is the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, a British Army corps

explanation.surface: An announcement of an attempt, with troops aboard an old vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the first piece is spoken; REME is a British Army corps, the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, familiar in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A trireme was an ancient Greek or Roman war galley with three banks of oars.

clue.text: Priest admitted to a slight desire

indicators.note: someone admitted to a place is let inside it, so one piece enters the other

blocks.note: taken as written
petite means slight or small in build
P is an abbreviation for priest

explanation.surface: A priest confesses to a small, forbidden longing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Admitted' suggests a confession, but it means let in: P goes between A and the word for slight.
explanation.definitionFit: An appetite is a craving or wish for something, especially food, and so a close synonym of desire.

clue.text: Distance at greens varies

indicators.note: something that varies changes form, so the letters take a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A golfer notes that the distance to the greens varies from hole to hole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Distance' looks like a noun about golf yardage, but it is a verb here, meaning to drive apart.
explanation.definitionFit: To estrange people is to alienate them and put emotional space between them, which is to distance them.

clue.text: Sits still at first, absorbing son's entrance

indicators.note: what comes at first is the opening letter, so only that is kept
to absorb is to take something in, so one piece holds another inside

blocks.note: someone who sits for a portrait poses
the opening letter of the word
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A model sits still at first while their son comes in through the entrance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entrance' looks like a noun for a doorway but is the verb en-TRANCE, to bewitch. The apostrophe-s after son means 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: To possess someone is to take hold of their mind, as a spirit does, which is to put them in a trance.

clue.text: Ancient Mariner's way to haul in a line

indicators.note: hauling something in pulls it inside, so one piece is drawn within another

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A description of how Coleridge's Ancient Mariner would pull in a fishing line.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital letters point to Coleridge's poem, but the definition is just any old sailor. The apostrophe-s means 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: An old salt is a seasoned sailor, so an ancient mariner is, in the crossword sense, a salt.

clue.text: Jack may be needed to fix this note

definitions.text: Jack may be needed to fix this

blocks.clueFragment: Jack may be needed to fix this
blocks.note: first meaning: a punctured tyre, fixed after raising the car on a jack
second meaning: a musical note lowered by a semitone

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests someone called Jack fixing a note, but a jack is the car tool; 'this' points forward to the second meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat is both a deflated tyre that needs changing and a musical note, such as B flat, pitched a semitone lower.

clue.text: Flaw in trial ordered in case of felony

indicators.note: something ordered is put into a new arrangement, so the letters are rearranged
the case of a word is its outside, so only its first and last letters are used
one thing in another sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: the outside letters of the word
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A legal flaw in a retrial ordered for a felony case.
explanation.walkthrough: The legal vocabulary ('trial', 'ordered', 'case', 'felony') all belongs to the courtroom, but only 'trial' supplies letters wholesale.
explanation.definitionFit: A frailty is a weakness of character or body, so it is a failing or flaw.

clue.text: Slashes independent firm first

indicators.note: saying one thing comes first sets the order, so the piece named before it is placed ahead

blocks.note: firm means solid
I is the abbreviation for independent

explanation.surface: An independent company slashes costs before anyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slashes' looks like a verb about cuts, but it is a plural noun for the / symbol. The firm piece comes before the independent one.
explanation.definitionFit: A solidus is the oblique stroke character, so solidi is the plural name for those typographic marks.

clue.text: The point of About a Boy

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
taken as written
a son is a boy

explanation.surface: A question about what Nick Hornby's novel About a Boy is really trying to say.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics make it a book title, but the three words split into separate pieces. About a Boy is a Nick Hornby novel, later a film.
explanation.definitionFit: The reason for something is its purpose or motive, as in asking what the point of it is.

clue.text: Conductor's lair

blocks.note: first meaning: the electrical connection to the ground
second meaning: a fox's burrow

explanation.walkthrough: 'Conductor' suggests an orchestra leader or bus conductor, but it is electrical: British wiring calls the ground wire the earth. A fox's den is also an earth.
explanation.definitionFit: Earth is both a conducting connection to the ground in a circuit and the underground home of a fox or badger.

clue.text: There's nothing in boy's mood that's attractive

definitions.note: the answer is a noun, a thing that attracts

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a boy is a lad; the possessive gives the S
O looks like zero, nothing
the tone of something is its mood

explanation.surface: Someone observes that a sulky boy's temper has no charm at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a noun phrase in disguise: 'that's attractive' means a thing that attracts. Loadstone is a variant spelling of lodestone.
explanation.definitionFit: A loadstone is a naturally magnetic piece of magnetite, which draws iron to it and so literally attracts.

clue.text: Hackneyed introduction to short story

indicators.note: an introduction comes at the start, so only the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
a tale is a story

explanation.surface: A critic dismisses the opening of a short story as clichéd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short story' reads as one literary form, but the first word only lends its initial.
explanation.definitionFit: Stale ideas or phrases are overused and no longer fresh, which is exactly what hackneyed means.

clue.text: Slight Roman gent scratching head

indicators.note: scratching out the head means striking off the front, so the first letter is removed

blocks.note: signore is the Italian for a gentleman, as one would address a man in Rome

explanation.surface: A slight Roman gentleman scratches his head in puzzlement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slight' looks like an adjective describing the gent, but it is the verb meaning to snub.
explanation.definitionFit: To slight someone is to snub or treat them with disregard, the same as to ignore them.

clue.text: Grubby theatres bound to be acquired by suits

indicators.note: something acquired is taken in by the buyer, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: to suit is to fit
a bound is a leap

explanation.surface: Run-down theatres are bound to be bought up by businessmen in suits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound to be' reads as 'certain to be', and 'suits' as executives; in fact 'bound' is a jump and 'suits' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Fleapit is British slang for a shabby, dirty old cinema or theatre, supposedly infested with fleas.

clue.text: All the same group of characters taken from Stevenson

indicators.note: a group of characters taken from a word is a run of letters lifted out of it

blocks.note: six consecutive letters inside the surname

explanation.surface: All the characters in one novel seem to come from the same Robert Louis Stevenson group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' suggests people in a Stevenson story such as Jekyll and Hyde, but here it means letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Even so is a phrase meaning nevertheless or despite that, a direct equivalent of all the same.

clue.text: Hire pony groomed for Titanic figure

indicators.note: grooming tidies and rearranges, so the letters are brushed into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A pony is hired and groomed to carry a very large rider.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Titanic' looks like 'huge' or a hint at the ship, but it means one of the Titans of Greek myth.
explanation.definitionFit: Hyperion was one of the Titans in Greek mythology, the father of Helios, the sun god.
